transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um, I hope I'm not taking up time someone else might need more, but... I guess I'm here because I've been losing chunks of time lately. It's a little embarrassing to admit, honestly. 

I just... I keep re-reading my emails and texts. Over and over. And I'll reopen folders on my computer right after I close them. I work in IT, so I'm at my desk a lot, but it's not really normal work stuff. And then, before I leave the house or start my work for the day, I find myself mentally replaying conversations. Like I'm going over everything I said. 

I think... well, it's like I’m just trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake. I know it probably sounds a bit silly. Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining this the right way.

Are these thoughts that come to you unwanted or intrusive, and do you feel like you have to do these repetitive actions or mental checks to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce your anxiety?

Well, yes, I suppose you could say they're unwanted. I certainly don't try to think about these things on purpose. It’s just... well, for example, even when I’m trying to focus and work through a system design, or prepare a lesson, this thought just keeps barging in. 

It's a little embarrassing to admit, honestly, but I'll suddenly worry that I might have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or maybe mishandled some family photos, or... or just let someone in the community down somehow. I know it's probably just me overthinking things, but I just can’t seem to let it pass. Even though I know I’ve been over it already, I end up doing those checks just to... well, to settle my nerves, I guess. 

I hope that makes sense? I really want to make sure I'm answering your questions correctly and giving you what you need.

When you do these mental checks or repetitive actions, like re-reading emails or replaying conversations, is it to try to prevent something bad from happening, or does it feel like something bad might happen if you don’t do them?

Um... well, I wouldn't really say it's a specific disaster or anything like that. I don't want you to think I'm completely losing touch with reality, you know? It's not like I believe someone is going to get hurt or something terrible will happen if I don't check my sent folder. 

It’s really just... I don't know, this nagging feeling. Like I just need to be absolutely sure I didn't make a foolish mistake. So I guess I'm not really trying to prevent a big bad event... I just want that uncomfortable, doubtful feeling to go away so I can get back to my day. 

Does that make sense? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of information here. I really want to be helpful.
Have you ever felt the need to do things in a certain way or order, or have you been unusually concerned about things like symmetry, cleanliness, or avoiding harm coming to yourself or others?

Oh, um, no, not really. I mean, I like things to be relatively tidy, just like anyone else, I suppose, but I'm definitely not overly concerned with cleaning or making sure things line up perfectly. If you saw my desk at work, you'd probably laugh—it's actually a bit cluttered with cables and notes. 

And like I was trying to say earlier, I don't really worry about people getting hurt or anything extreme like that. It's really just the checking... the emails and replaying those conversations. 

I hope that's okay? I mean, I hope I'm not making this confusing for you by not having those other issues. Am I still giving you the right kind of information? I just want to make sure I'm doing this right.
Do these thoughts or the need to check things cause you a lot of anxiety or distress, even if you know the chances of something being wrong are very low?

Well, I wouldn't say it's a *lot* of distress. I mean, I don't want to sound like I'm falling apart or anything, because I'm really not. I still get my work done and everything. 

It's more just... annoying, I guess? Like, I know the chances of me actually sending a horrible email to my ex-wife are basically zero, but the thought just kind of sticks there until I double-check. It does make me a little anxious, sure, but I can handle it. It's just a mild frustration, really. 

I hope that's not disappointing? I mean, I know you're looking for how much it bothers me, and I don't want to make it sound like it's nothing, but I also don't want to exaggerate. Am I explaining that in a way that's helpful for your notes?
Do these checking behaviors take up a lot of your time during the day, or do they interfere with your work, relationships, or other important activities?

Um, well... I wouldn't say it takes up a *lot* of time. I mean, I'm still getting my main tasks done, mostly. I really don't want you to think I'm slacking off at my job or anything like that. 

But, I guess... well, if I'm being completely honest, it has slowed me down a bit lately. Like, I've missed a couple of design milestones recently, which isn't really like me. And I've had to push back some mentoring sessions with the junior devs that I usually handle without any problem. It's just that the checking kind of eats into my schedule more than I expect it to. 

And... there was this one thing outside of work. I volunteer at a youth coding workshop—it's something I really care about. But last week, I was late and completely unprepared because I got stuck re-reading a bunch of emails before I left the house. I felt really terrible and embarrassed about that. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound completely incompetent? I'm really trying to keep everything on track, I promise. Is that the kind of example you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you a clear picture without making it sound worse than it is.
Have you ever had thoughts about harming yourself or someone else, even if you wouldn’t actually act on them?

Oh, gosh, no. No, absolutely not. I would never want to hurt anyone, and definitely not myself. I really hope I haven't given you the impression that I'm dangerous or unstable in that way, because I'm really not. 

I mean, the only thoughts I have are just those silly worries about accidentally sending the wrong email, like I mentioned. But nothing violent or... or scary like that. I'm actually a very calm person, usually. 

I hope it's okay that I don't have those kinds of thoughts? I know you have to ask these things to be thorough, and I want to make sure I'm answering correctly. Am I still being helpful even if I don't have those specific issues?

When you're doing these checks—like re-reading emails or replaying conversations—does it feel like you have to do them in order to stop feeling anxious or uncomfortable, even if you know the chances of something being wrong are low?

Well, yes, I suppose that's a fair way to put it. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm completely overwhelmed by anxiety, but... yeah, it does feel like I have to do it just to settle my mind. 

It's actually the main reason I decided to come in and talk to someone. I just... I keep losing these chunks of time, you know? Like, I'll be re-reading emails and texts, or reopening folders on my computer, or just kind of mentally replaying conversations in my head before I leave the house or start my work for the day. 

It's like I'm just trying to prove to myself that I didn't make some serious mistake, even though I know I probably didn't. I just want to be absolutely sure so I don't cause any problems for anyone else. I really try to be conscientious about my work and my interactions. 

I hope that makes sense? I know it probably sounds a bit silly, spending all that time just to feel comfortable. I really hope you don't think I'm just being completely neurotic or wasting my time on purpose. Is that the kind of feeling you were asking about?
Do you feel distressed specifically when you’re unable to complete your checking behaviors, even if you know there’s probably nothing wrong?

Well, um... 'distressed' might be a slightly strong word? I really don't want to sound like I fall apart or anything if I can't do it. I try very hard to stay professional and keep it together. 

But... yes, I suppose if I'm being completely honest, it is really uncomfortable. Like I was just mentioning a moment ago about why I came in—losing all that time reopening those folders and re-reading texts just to prove to myself I didn't make a serious mistake... if I'm interrupted and I *can't* finish doing that before I start work, it does bother me quite a bit. 

It just sort of gnaws at me. I try my absolute best to hide it so I don't inconvenience anyone or make a fuss, but it's really hard to focus on whatever I'm supposed to be doing until I can go back and finish checking. I hope it's okay to admit that? I just want to make sure I'm doing a good job and not causing problems for my team or my family. Did I explain that clearly enough for your notes? I want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need.

Have you ever had persistent thoughts about things needing to be done in a very specific or exact way, or have you felt upset if something didn’t feel quite right, even if it wasn’t about making a mistake or checking something?

Oh, no, not really. I mean, I like things to be neat and tidy, of course—I think most people do, right? Especially working with computers, you sort of have to be a little organized. But I don't have any strict rules or... or weird rituals about how things have to be arranged or anything like that. 

I really try to be flexible and easygoing. If someone moves a pen on my desk or if a picture frame is slightly crooked, it doesn't upset me. I wouldn't want to be one of those people who makes everyone around them miserable because things aren't perfect. I'm very easy to work with, I promise. 

So, no, it's really just the checking things that I mentioned before. I hope that's an okay answer? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information. I'm not trying to be difficult by not having those other symptoms, I just want to be completely honest with you. Is that helpful?
Have you ever had any other recurring thoughts, urges, or images that feel intrusive and unwanted, or felt driven to perform any other behaviors or mental acts in response to those thoughts?

Well, um... I guess there is one other thing. I really don't want it to sound like my mind is completely out of control, because it's not, I promise. I can still do my job and everything. But... yeah, sometimes I do get these thoughts that just sort of barge in when I don't want them to. 

Like, I'll be right in the middle of trying to work through a system design, or maybe preparing a lesson, and suddenly I just get this... this really persistent thought that I might have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or maybe I mishandled some old family photos, or somehow let someone down in the community. 

And I know I've already been over it, and I try to just tell myself, 'You've checked this, it's fine,' but... I just can't seem to let it pass. It just kind of sits there, nagging at me. I really try to just push it away and focus on my work, because I don't want to be distracted or do a bad job. 

I hope it doesn't make me sound completely unhinged to admit that? I know everyone worries sometimes, and I'm probably just making a mountain out of a molehill. But that is the kind of thing you were asking about, right? I just want to be sure I'm answering your questions properly.

When you perform these checking behaviors, do you feel that they are necessary to prevent something bad from happening to you or someone else, even if you know that they might not logically prevent it?

Well, um... no, not exactly. I don't think so, anyway. I'm really not worried that if I don't check my files or my messages, someone is going to get physically hurt or, you know, some terrible tragedy is going to strike my family. It's nothing dramatic like that. 

I mean, I know some people might feel that way, and I really hope it doesn't mess up your evaluation or your notes that I don't have that specific worry. I'm just... it's really just about me not wanting to have made a stupid mistake. I just want to be absolutely sure I didn't mess up a project at work or accidentally offend someone, because I'd hate to be a burden or cause trouble for anyone else. 

So it's not really about preventing a disaster, just... preventing myself from looking foolish or letting people down, I guess? Does that make sense? I hope I'm not being difficult by saying no to that one, I just want to make sure I'm giving you the exact right picture of what's going on so I don't waste your time.
When you're unable to finish checking your emails or replaying conversations in your mind, does it cause you significant anxiety or discomfort that’s hard to ignore?

Well, um... I wouldn't really say it causes *significant* anxiety. I definitely don't want to give you the impression that I'm falling apart over it or anything like that. 

If I get interrupted—like if a colleague comes over to my desk while I'm double-checking my outbox, or if I'm trying to think through a conversation and the phone rings—it's maybe a little annoying? Just like leaving any job half-finished, you know? I might feel a tiny bit unsettled, but it's certainly not some unbearable panic that I can't ignore. 

I can just put a pin in it, smile, and talk to whoever needs me. I'm always very polite, and I really try to keep it under wraps so it doesn't bother anyone else in the office. I just go back and finish checking later when I have a quiet minute. 

I hope it's okay that I don't get super anxious about it? I know you're looking for how these things affect me, and I'm really trying to be a good patient and give you what you need. Is it alright that it just feels more like a mild annoyance rather than major distress? I hope I'm not messing up your evaluation by not having that intense reaction.
Do you often find yourself worrying about a variety of different things, like work, family, or other responsibilities, even when there isn't a specific reason to be concerned?

Well, um... no, not really. I mean, I try to stay on top of things, of course. I like to be prepared for work and make sure my family is doing okay, but I wouldn't say I just sit around worrying about everything all the time for no reason. 

I really hope that's the right kind of answer? I just don't want you to think I'm a nervous wreck about every little thing in my life, because I'm honestly not. I try to handle my responsibilities pretty well, and I don't want to come across as someone who can't cope with normal day-to-day stuff. 

So, no, it's really just those specific things I mentioned before, not a general worry about everything. I hope that makes sense and helps with your notes? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the clearest picture possible.

My symptom profile includes obsessions (S065) about making mistakes (sending wrong messages, mishandling photos) and compulsions (S066) of checking, but it does not include symmetry or 'just right' obsessions.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, not really. I mean, I like things to be neat and tidy, of course—I think most people do, right? Especially working with computers, you sort of have to be a little organized. But I don't have any strict rules or... or weird rituals about how things have to be arranged or anything like that. 

I really try to be flexible and easygoing. If someone moves a pen on my desk or if a picture frame is slightly crooked, it doesn't upset me. I wouldn't want to be one of those people who makes everyone around them miserable because things aren't perfect. I'm very easy to work with, I promise. 

So, no, it's really just the checking things that I mentioned before. I hope that's an okay answer? I want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information. I'm not trying to be difficult by not having those other symptoms, I just want to be completely honest with you. Is that helpful?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any additional obsessions or compulsions beyond checking, which would support a diagnosis of OCD (F42.2) over Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1)
doctor.question: Have you ever had any other recurring thoughts, urges, or images that feel intrusive and unwanted, or felt driven to perform any other behaviors or mental acts in response to those thoughts?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: Even when I’m trying to work through a system design or prepare a lesson, this thought keeps barging in that I may have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, mishandled some family photos, or let someone in the community down, and I can’t seem to let it pass even though I know I’ve been over it already.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recurring thoughts, urges, or images that feel intrusive and unwanted, which directly corresponds to the definition of Obsessions (S065).

patient.answer:
Well, um... I guess there is one other thing. I really don't want it to sound like my mind is completely out of control, because it's not, I promise. I can still do my job and everything. But... yeah, sometimes I do get these thoughts that just sort of barge in when I don't want them to. 

Like, I'll be right in the middle of trying to work through a system design, or maybe preparing a lesson, and suddenly I just get this... this really persistent thought that I might have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or maybe I mishandled some old family photos, or somehow let someone down in the community. 

And I know I've already been over it, and I try to just tell myself, 'You've checked this, it's fine,' but... I just can't seem to let it pass. It just kind of sits there, nagging at me. I really try to just push it away and focus on my work, because I don't want to be distracted or do a bad job. 

I hope it doesn't make me sound completely unhinged to admit that? I know everyone worries sometimes, and I'm probably just making a mountain out of a molehill. But that is the kind of thing you were asking about, right? I just want to be sure I'm answering your questions properly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsions that are aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or distress, even if they recognize that the compulsions are excessive or not realistically connected to the feared event.
doctor.question: When you perform these checking behaviors, do you feel that they are necessary to prevent something bad from happening to you or someone else, even if you know that they might not logically prevent it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about magical thinking or beliefs that checking behaviors prevent harm (which relates to the 'prevent anxiety/distress or some dreaded event' part of compulsions or specific types of obsessions), but my profile does not explicitly mention doing things to prevent harm to myself or others; my compulsions are about trying to prove I didn't make a serious mistake.

patient.answer:
Well, um... no, not exactly. I don't think so, anyway. I'm really not worried that if I don't check my files or my messages, someone is going to get physically hurt or, you know, some terrible tragedy is going to strike my family. It's nothing dramatic like that. 

I mean, I know some people might feel that way, and I really hope it doesn't mess up your evaluation or your notes that I don't have that specific worry. I'm just... it's really just about me not wanting to have made a stupid mistake. I just want to be absolutely sure I didn't mess up a project at work or accidentally offend someone, because I'd hate to be a burden or cause trouble for anyone else. 

So it's not really about preventing a disaster, just... preventing myself from looking foolish or letting people down, I guess? Does that make sense? I hope I'm not being difficult by saying no to that one, I just want to make sure I'm giving you the exact right picture of what's going on so I don't waste your time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety or distress specifically when unable to complete checking behaviors, which would support OCD (F42.2) over GAD (F41.1).
doctor.question: When you're unable to finish checking your emails or replaying conversations in your mind, does it cause you significant anxiety or discomfort that’s hard to ignore?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the emotional response (anxiety/discomfort) when unable to complete the compulsions. The provided symptom profiles cover the obsessions (S065), the compulsions themselves (S066), and functional impairment, but do not specifically cover the anxiety or distress caused by being unable to perform the compulsions.

patient.answer:
Well, um... I wouldn't really say it causes *significant* anxiety. I definitely don't want to give you the impression that I'm falling apart over it or anything like that. 

If I get interrupted—like if a colleague comes over to my desk while I'm double-checking my outbox, or if I'm trying to think through a conversation and the phone rings—it's maybe a little annoying? Just like leaving any job half-finished, you know? I might feel a tiny bit unsettled, but it's certainly not some unbearable panic that I can't ignore. 

I can just put a pin in it, smile, and talk to whoever needs me. I'm always very polite, and I really try to keep it under wraps so it doesn't bother anyone else in the office. I just go back and finish checking later when I have a quiet minute. 

I hope it's okay that I don't get super anxious about it? I know you're looking for how these things affect me, and I'm really trying to be a good patient and give you what you need. Is it alright that it just feels more like a mild annoyance rather than major distress? I hope I'm not messing up your evaluation by not having that intense reaction.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder, such as persistent worry about various events or activities, which may help differentiate between F42.2 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder) and F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder).
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself worrying about a variety of different things, like work, family, or other responsibilities, even when there isn't a specific reason to be concerned?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about Generalized Anxiety Disorder symptoms (worrying about a variety of different things like work, family, etc., without specific reason), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, um... no, not really. I mean, I try to stay on top of things, of course. I like to be prepared for work and make sure my family is doing okay, but I wouldn't say I just sit around worrying about everything all the time for no reason. 

I really hope that's the right kind of answer? I just don't want you to think I'm a nervous wreck about every little thing in my life, because I'm honestly not. I try to handle my responsibilities pretty well, and I don't want to come across as someone who can't cope with normal day-to-day stuff. 

So, no, it's really just those specific things I mentioned before, not a general worry about everything. I hope that makes sense and helps with your notes? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the clearest picture possible.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms are primarily centered around checking behaviors related to intrusive thoughts about potential mistakes, without broader anxiety or generalized worry. The absence of significant distress, symmetry concerns, or other compulsions supports ruling out F41.1. The checking behaviors are driven by an urge to neutralize uncertainty/distress, aligning with OCD, and the lack of other major anxiety features makes F42.2 the most precise fit.
